question: What distinguishes an abstract class from an interface in modern Java?
option_a: An abstract class can hold state (instance fields) and concrete methods; an interface traditionally declares abstract contracts (with static/default methods allowed)
option_b: Interfaces can have fields with values

question: String a = "PGI"; String b = "PGI"; Which is TRUE about a == b in Java?
option_a: true, because both refer to the same interned string literal in the constant pool
option_d: true only if using new String
explanation: String literals are interned: identical literals share one object, so == (reference equality) returns true. new String("PGI") would create a distinct object.

question: Why is String immutable in Java?
option_a: For security, caching/hash-code stability, thread safety and reuse in the string pool
option_d: Only to save memory in one case
explanation: Immutability gives safe sharing, reliable hashCode, thread safety and pool reuse. StringBuilder/StringBuffer exist for mutable text.

question: When you call start() on a Thread object, the JVM:
option_a: Creates a new thread and invokes run() in it
option_b: Directly calls run() in the current thread
explanation: start() spawns a new thread of execution that runs run(). Calling run() directly executes it synchronously in the calling thread, not in a new thread.
